visible_changes.before: Mean quantile loss and breach frequency answer different questions. The two H6 FX comparisons reduce U and V despite more strict breaches; their sample-average improvement persists under every constant nonnegative linear weighting of those components. Higher breach frequency rules out empirical first-order stochastic dominance in the favorable direction for the distribution of positive-part errors (P−C)<sub>+</sub>, including zeros: its empirical distribution function is lower at zero. A cost per breach or a nonlinear loss can therefore change the ranking. The smaller H24 FX legacy gain instead trades increased U for reduced V and reverses at ratio 20.63. These are properties of fixed reports under stipulated weights, rather than measured financing costs or uniformly improved tail risk.
visible_changes.after: Mean quantile loss and breach frequency answer different questions. The two H6 FX comparisons reduce U and V despite more strict breaches; their sample-average loss is lower under every constant nonnegative linear weighting of those components with at least one positive weight. Higher breach frequency rules out empirical first-order stochastic dominance in the favorable direction for the distribution of positive-part errors (P−C)<sub>+</sub>, including zeros: its empirical distribution function is lower at zero. A cost per breach or a nonlinear loss can therefore change the ranking. The smaller H24 FX legacy gain instead trades increased U for reduced V and reverses at ratio 20.63. These are properties of fixed reports under stipulated weights, rather than measured financing costs or uniformly improved tail risk.
